source.title: On the Complexity of Neural Computation in Superposition

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical constructions and bounds for computing sparse Boolean features in superposition, rather than reproducing the original toy-model training and measurement procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper's own constructions and analyses are recorded below. Statements about Claude 3 Sonnet, SAEs, and subsequent trained-network work are cited or discussed rather than results produced here; the LLM extension in Appendix A.2 is explicitly hypothetical.
record.test_reason: The paper is purely theoretical. It takes superposition and feature sparsity as premises and proves bounds on neurons and parameters needed to compute Boolean functions in superposition. It trains no network and measures no learned representation. Its random-code overlap bound (R1) holds by construction, so it shows nothing about whether trained networks store features this way. None of V1–V6 concerns computational capacity, so its results fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim the first subexponential capacity bound: n neurons compute at most O(n²/log n) features. They also claim parameter count is a good estimator of the number of features a network computes. The claim that output channels emerge in trained toy networks is cited from later work (Adler et al. 2025), not shown here.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses hand-designed random-compression ReLU networks and information-theoretic parameter-counting bounds for Boolean computation, rather than training toy models to study representational geometry or sparsity-dependent transitions.
record.method_sensitivity: The constructions use different algorithms according to feature influence (low, high, or mixed). The paper also states that allowing v active inputs incurs an additional complexity factor with exponential dependence on v.

fits_no_version.finding: Computing m′ sparse Boolean outputs (2-AND, permutation) in superposition requires Ω(m′ log m′) parameter bits. In the square-matrix model that means Ω(√(m′ log m′)) neurons. Explicit ReLU constructions nearly match this bound. The paper contrasts this with O(log m′) neurons for passive representation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Active computation in superposition has far lower feature capacity than passive representation: n neurons compute at most O(n²/log n) features of these function classes.

fits_no_version.finding: Random Bernoulli codes give unit-diagonal, O(1/log m) off-diagonal overlap with n = Θ(√(m log m)), so sparse inputs can be recovered by thresholding. This is a design property.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constructive existence of near-orthogonal sparse codes supporting superposed representation, not evidence about trained networks.

record.problems: The results concern structured Boolean functions and hand-designed constructions, not trained neural networks or LLMs. The main constructions assume at most two active inputs; the extension to more active inputs has an exponential dependence on the sparsity parameter. The paper itself notes that its abstractions limit direct scope and that the sharpest lower bounds rely on ordered outputs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for cited empirical work or the hypothetical LLM lower-bound discussion in Appendix A.2; those are not original results of this study. No further own reported results bearing on the listed versions were omitted.

untested.parts: All parts. There are no trained toy models, no sparsity-dependent phase transition and no learned geometry. The near-orthogonal codes are hand-built.
All parts. There is no analysis of importance-based allocation to dedicated versus shared dimensions.
All parts. There are no LLM measurements, and the Appendix A.2 LLM extension is hypothetical.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 'supports' label is removed. The encoding overlap bound is engineered by the authors, not observed in a trained system. Superposition is the paper's premise rather than its object of test.

versions.untested_parts: Tests hand-designed random-compression representations and computation for Boolean inputs with at most two active features. Does not test trained toy networks, a sparsity-dependent transition, or a general regular geometry beyond the stated random-code overlap bounds.
No experiment or analysis of importance-based allocation into dedicated versus shared neuron dimensions, or of polysemanticity as a cause of capacity competition.
Does not test whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.
No original LLM measurement of feature spread across neurons or SAE-recoverable sparse features; cited examples are not this study's results.
Does not test SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
Does not test whether features in superposition are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional objects.

rows.subject: Bernoulli compression C with decompressor D
rows.size_stated: n = Θ(√(m log m)); input dimension m
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed the encoding and decompression overlap R = DC for random Bernoulli compression.

conditions.value: At most 2 active inputs in the construction assumptions

rows.measure: Off-diagonal entries of R; diagonal entries are 1.
rows.uncertainty: w.h.p.; defined in the paper as probability at least 1 − m^−α for an arbitrary constant α > 0, with adjusted constants
rows.note: This is a bound on encoding/decompression cross-talk in the constructed sparse representation, not a measurement of trained-network feature directions.
rows.check: A designed property of the authors' own random Bernoulli encoder: nearly orthogonal codes exist, a Johnson-Lindenstrauss-style fact. It does not observe trained toy models storing features this way, nor a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry. It should not be linked to V1.

rows.note: A constructed algorithm, not a trained-network observation.
rows.check: A correctness and neuron-count guarantee for the authors' own construction. It is not a measurement of any version's effect.
